sections.h2: Miami County, Ohio: parcels and school districts
sections.html:
Miami County belongs to the Dayton metropolitan area, with Shelby County to the north, Champaign and Clark to the east, Montgomery to the south and Darke to the west. The auditor counts 54,707 parcels. Troy holds the courthouse and is the largest city, Piqua and Tipp City are cities too, and Huber Heights and Union each extend partly into the county.

Troy, Piqua, Tipp City, Covington, Milton-Union, Miami East, Newton, Bradford and Bethel each have their own public school district. The district that serves a house decides several of the levies printed on its bill, so name it in any listing conversation about taxes.

The county had 112,634 residents in July 2025, 3.5 percent more than at the 2020 base. Nearly three in four households (73.4 percent) own, among 44,906 households in all.

  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $229,100.
  • Monthly owner costs run $1,453 with a mortgage and $549 without one.
  • Gross rent is $966 at the median.
  • Household income is $76,817 at the median.
  • Permits for 340 new units were issued in 2025, against 47,930 housing units overall.

About a quarter of occupied homes are rentals, so a sale with a tenant in place is nothing unusual in Troy or Piqua.

sections.h2: How the auditor sets a value
sections.html:
Ohio requires a full reappraisal every sixth year, plus an update at the midpoint, and the taxable base is set at 35 percent of market value. A record for each parcel sits in the auditor's office and anyone may inspect it. Ask which year brings the next update.

The auditor cannot change a tax rate. Rates reflect budget requests by local governments and votes by residents, and a bill equals the rate times the valuation on the general tax list. Absent a vote, Ohio limits taxation to ten mills. Every levy beyond that was approved at the polls. Special assessments for ditches, paving, curbs, sidewalks, sewers or water lines show up as their own line on the bill.

Before you list, pull your parcel record from the auditor's office and read it. A wrong square footage, room count or condition entry can inflate the value, and fixing it is easier before a buyer asks about the tax bill.

The treasurer collects real estate tax in two installments, February 14 and July 20, and the printed statement carries the exact dates. A postmark on the due date counts as on time.

Miami County tax collection dates and penalties

The treasurer works from the Safety Building, 201 W. Main Street in Troy, phone (937) 440-6045. You can mail a payment with the bill stub, come to the counter on weekdays between eight and four, or use the night deposit box on the building's east side. Card payments go through an outside processor that adds 2.50 percent, and eChecks add a flat $1.99.

Owners who fell behind can ask the office about a delinquent payment contract. Ohio law also permits tax lien certificate sales under section 5721.32 of the Revised Code.

sections.h2: Tax breaks for Miami County homeowners
sections.html:
Almost every program below is filed with the auditor.

  • Owner occupancy credit: available if you own the house and treat it as your main home on the January 1 that starts the filing year. It reaches the dwelling plus one acre and is often completed during the transfer.
  • Non-business credit: limited to residential and farm levies that predate the November 2013 election.
  • Homestead exemption: for homeowners aged 65 and up, or permanently disabled, who live in the house. Filing opens the first Monday of January and closes the first Monday of June, and new applicants take an income test.
  • Surviving spouse of a public service officer: a $58,000 reduction with no income limit when the officer died in the line of duty.
  • Current agricultural use value: for ten or more acres in commercial farming, or smaller tracts averaging $2,500 a year in gross income, with filing from the first Monday of January to the first Monday of March.

Phone the auditor at (937) 440-5925 to learn the homestead income limit.

The Board of Revision takes valuation complaints. The auditor is its permanent secretary, joined by the treasurer and the commissioners' president. Submit DTE Form 1, the Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, to the auditor from January 1 through March 31.

The board then sends a decision or schedules a hearing. A complaint challenges the assessed value and cannot touch the millage rate, which comes from local governments and voters. Gather sales of similar homes, an independent appraisal or photographs. An appraisal strengthens a case but is optional.

Mobile homes follow their own calendar, with the first half due March 1 and the second July 31. Owners of manufactured homes register them with the auditor, who assesses each home yearly and bills twice a year. The revenue is shared among townships, cities and schools just as real estate tax is.

Farmland follows another path. The auditor administers the current agricultural use value program, which the Ohio Department of Taxation oversees through soil rate values. In a reappraisal year, applications may be taken all year. Leaving agricultural use can change how land is valued, so talk to the auditor before listing a farm tract.

sections.h2: Transfer fees and selling with taxes owed
sections.html:
The auditor charges $2.00 for each thousand dollars of price, plus 50 cents per parcel for transfer. A check must match the amount to the penny or the conveyance is not processed. Ordinary sales go in on DTE Form 100, and exempt transfers on Form 100 (EX). A fee calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

The recorder, auditor and engineer jointly adopted conveyance standards, and ORC 317.114 has governed recorded documents since July 1, 2009. Before closing, get the tax payoff from the treasurer and ask the closing agent how the current bill is shared. If the buyer will occupy the house, the owner occupancy application is frequently filed with the transfer.

If taxes are past due, the payoff comes out of your sale proceeds at closing. A cash buyer does not change that, though a cash sale can close faster, so request the payoff early and ask the treasurer about any penalty already added.

faqs.q: Which day is the Miami County second installment due?
faqs.a: July 20. The February installment is due on the 14th, and the statement carries exact dates. A payment postmarked by the deadline counts as timely.

faqs.q: How much are late payment penalties in Miami County?
faqs.a: Five percent in the first ten days after the deadline, then 10 percent on unpaid current tax. The treasurer's office offers delinquent payment contracts.

faqs.q: What window applies to a Miami County valuation complaint?
faqs.a: January 1 through March 31, on DTE Form 1 filed with the county auditor. The Board of Revision then rules or schedules a formal hearing.

faqs.q: What fees go with a Miami County deed transfer?
faqs.a: The auditor charges $2.00 per thousand dollars of price and 50 cents per parcel, paid by a check for the exact amount. Use DTE Form 100, or Form 100 (EX) for an exempt transfer.

faqs.q: Where does a Miami County senior apply for the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Apply at the auditor's office between the first Monday of January and the first Monday of June. Applicants need to be 65 or over, or permanently disabled, and live in the house. Call (937) 440-5925 about the income test.
